title: Palantir's Alex Karp says AI's biggest names may never IPO — the play is telling Washington 'nationalize us, please'
excerpt: More government oversight could be better for humanity, but also serves to cover AI companies’ butts.
content_html:
The current and former tech staffers who blew the whistle on AI's ability to "kill us all" have had the internet abuzz since they made their revelations earlier this month, eventually spurring Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic head Dario Amodei to issue a joint call for the sector to ease up on the gas pedal.

But, there have been questions about the mixed motivations of tightening regulation surrounding emerging innovations, which could put greater control — and with it, more profits — in the hands of certain individuals and/or companies.

  • Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

  • Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

  • A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

New statements from Alex Karp at Palantir, a company that provides bridging software for cognitive computing programs, suggest further options of where experts see the industry going, up to and including complete government takeover to ensure public safety.

In an interview with CNBC on September 17, the chief executive spoke about how some of the aforementioned companies may soon be begging to nationalize; not necessarily just for the good of humanity, but to assuage the tremendous liability that they are now facing.

'Reasonable guidelines' for 'unlimited' risk

"These businesses have to be nationalized because if you don't nationalize it, every single one of [their] clients is going to sue," Karp said.

He also advocated for the Fed to impose a framework for greater civil and criminal punishments if and when firms developing machine learning "aren't being responsible."

"The first line of defense is you're liable for your own actions. So it's a weird twist they're asking for societal regulations to get out of the first line of defense, which is if you build a technology that can destroy 10% of the world, that has civil and criminal liability attached to it," he noted.

But, interestingly, his comments also serve Palantir's own interests, as he has preached about the need for greater AI sovereignty and oversight — which Palantir offers solutions for, of course.
